content: Mentha, commonly known as mint, is a genus comprising approximately 25 species of flowering plants, along with numerous varieties, belonging to the family Lamiaceae. These species are distributed across various regions of the world, including Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia, and North America. Hybridization is common among mint species, resulting in several naturally occurring hybrids. Mint plants are aromatic herbs, predominantly perennial, with only a few annual species. They possess extensive underground rhizomes and upright, branched stems. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and vary in shape from simple oblong to lanceolate. They are often covered with fine hairs and have serrated edges. The color of the leaves ranges from dark green and gray-green to shades of purple, blue, and occasionally pale yellow. The genus Mentha includes a selection of species considered to be pure mints. However, as with all plant classifications, the list of recognized species is subject to change. Accepted species names, along with their common names, are documented, and synonyms, cultivars, and varieties are listed under each species where applicable. Mint hybrids are abundant within the mint family, and their classification is also subject to updates. Synonyms, cultivars, and varieties are included under specific hybrid species. Mint plants thrive in cool, moist environments with partial shade, although they can tolerate a wide range of conditions, including full sun. They grow rapidly, spreading through a network of runners. Due to their vigorous growth, a single plant of each desired mint variety, with minimal care, can provide sufficient mint for home use. However, some mint species are more invasive than others. Even less invasive varieties can dominate other plants if not managed carefully. To control their spread, mints should be planted in deep, bottomless containers sunk into the ground or grown above ground in tubs or barrels. Propagation of mint can be achieved through seeds, but this method is often unreliable due to the high variability of mint seeds and the sterility of some varieties. A more effective approach is to propagate mint by planting cuttings taken from the runners of healthy plants. Popular mint varieties for cultivation include peppermint (Mentha × piperita), spearmint (Mentha spicata), and pineapple mint (Mentha suaveolens). Mints are excellent companion plants, repelling pest insects and attracting beneficial ones. For example, spearmint and peppermint are often grown alongside tomato and pepper plants to enhance flavor, repel aphids, attract parasitic wasps that prey on caterpillars, and provide ground cover as living mulch. Chamomile is also considered a good companion plant for mint, as it is believed to increase the essential oil content in mint, enhancing its aroma and flavor. Mint leaves can be harvested at any time. Fresh mint leaves should be used immediately or stored for a few days in plastic bags within a refrigerator. Alternatively, mint can be frozen in ice cube trays. Dried mint leaves should be stored in an airtight container in a cool, dark, and dry area. Fresh mint is generally preferred over dried mint when storage is not an issue. The leaves have a pleasant, warm, fresh, aromatic, and sweet flavor with a cool aftertaste. Mint leaves are used in teas, beverages, jellies, syrups, candies, and ice creams. In Middle Eastern cuisine, mint is commonly used in lamb dishes, while in British cuisine, mint sauce is a popular accompaniment to lamb. Mint is an essential ingredient in Touareg tea, a traditional tea in northern African and Arab countries. Mint is also featured in alcoholic beverages such as the Mint Julep and Mojito. Mint essential oil and menthol are widely used as flavorings in breath fresheners, drinks, antiseptic mouth rinses, toothpaste, chewing gum, and desserts. The characteristic aromas and flavors of mints are attributed to compounds such as menthol (the primary aroma in spearmint, peppermint, and Japanese peppermint), pulegone (found in pennyroyal and Corsican mint), and methyl salicylate (commonly known as oil of wintergreen, used as a mint flavoring in foods and candies). Mints also serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, such as the Buff Ermine moth. Historically, mint was used as a medicinal herb to treat stomach aches and chest pains. During the Middle Ages, powdered mint leaves were employed to whiten teeth. Mint tea is a potent diuretic and aids digestion. Menthol, derived from mint essential oil, is a key ingredient in many cosmetics and perfumes. It is also extensively used in medicine as a component of various drugs and is popular in aromatherapy. Menthol is commonly used as an antipruritic, particularly in treatments for insect bites, often in combination with camphor. Additionally, menthol is used as an additive in cigarettes to mask the bitter taste of tobacco and soothe the throat. The strong, sharp flavor and scent of mint are believed to act as a mild decongestant for illnesses such as the common cold. In ancient Rome, Pliny recommended that students wear a wreath of mint to exhilarate their minds, a suggestion supported by some modern research. Mint leaves are often used by campers to repel mosquitoes. Extracts from mint leaves are also reported to have mosquito-killing properties. Mint oil is employed as an environmentally friendly insecticide, effective against pests such as wasps, hornets, ants, and cockroaches. The word mint originates from the Latin term mentha, which is derived from the Greek word minthe. In Greek mythology, Minthe was the name of a woman associated with the plant. In Central and South America, mint is referred to as hierbabuena, meaning good herb. In Hindi and Urdu, it is called Pudina. The taxonomic family Lamiaceae, known as the mint family, includes many other aromatic herbs commonly used in cooking, such as basil, rosemary, sage, oregano, and catnip. In English colloquial usage, mint can refer to any small sugar confectionery item flavored to resemble the plant. However, some plants with fragrant leaves are mistakenly called mint, such as Vietnamese mint, which is not a member of the mint family. In New Zealand, mint is also used as an exclamation, as in mint.
